questions.stem: Newton's law of viscosity states that the shear stress in a fluid is proportional to the:
questions.solution:
**The RATE of shear strain — the velocity gradient du/dy.**

> **τ = μ (du/dy)**

**This is the defining difference between a fluid and a solid**, and it is worth stating precisely:

| | **SOLID** | **FLUID** |
|---|---|---|
| Stress is proportional to | **STRAIN** (Hooke: τ = G γ) | **RATE OF STRAIN** (Newton: τ = μ dγ/dt) |
| Under a constant shear stress | Deforms a **finite amount** and **stops** | **Deforms CONTINUOUSLY** — it flows |
| At rest | Can sustain shear | **Cannot sustain any shear stress** |

> **A fluid is a substance that DEFORMS CONTINUOUSLY under ANY shear stress, however small.** That is the definition, and everything else follows from it.

**The consequence for a fluid at rest** is immediate and is the foundation of hydrostatics:

> If a fluid at rest could sustain shear it would flow — so **a fluid at rest has NO shear stress**, and the only stress is the **normal** stress, which is the **pressure**. That is why hydrostatic pressure acts **equally in all directions** (Pascal's law).

**Dynamic viscosity μ:**

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| **SI unit** | **Pa·s** = N·s/m² = kg/(m·s) |
| **CGS unit** | **poise** (P); **1 Pa·s = 10 poise** |
| Water at 20 °C | **1.0 × 10⁻³ Pa·s** = 1 centipoise |
| Air at 20 °C | 1.8 × 10⁻⁵ Pa·s |

**Kinematic viscosity ν = μ/ρ**, with SI unit **m²/s** and CGS unit **stokes** (1 m²/s = 10⁴ stokes). Water at 20 °C: **1.0 × 10⁻⁶ m²/s**.

**Note that air is about 55 times LESS viscous than water in DYNAMIC terms but about 15 times MORE viscous in KINEMATIC terms** — because air's density is so much lower. Which viscosity matters depends on the problem: **dynamic** viscosity governs the shear stress, **kinematic** viscosity governs the diffusion of momentum and appears in the Reynolds number.

**Fluid classification by the τ – du/dy relationship:**

| Type | Behaviour | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **NEWTONIAN** | **τ ∝ du/dy**, straight line **through the origin** | **Water, air, oil**, most common fluids |
| **Dilatant** (shear-thickening) | Viscosity **increases** with shear rate | Starch suspension, wet sand |
| **Pseudoplastic** (shear-thinning) | Viscosity **decreases** with shear rate | Paint, blood, polymer solutions |
| **BINGHAM PLASTIC** | Needs a **YIELD STRESS** before flowing at all | **Toothpaste, drilling mud, fresh CONCRETE, sewage sludge** |
| Ideal fluid | **μ = 0**, no shear stress ever | A **hypothetical** fluid; a useful idealisation |

**The Bingham plastic is the one a civil engineer meets most often**: **fresh concrete** will not flow until the applied stress exceeds a yield value, which is exactly why it can be placed on a slope and hold its shape, and why the **slump test** measures something meaningful.

examTip.trap: "Shear strain" is the deliberate near-miss — that is **Hooke's law for a SOLID**. A fluid responds to the **rate** of strain.
examTip.trick: That one word is the whole definition of a fluid: a solid deforms a finite amount and stops; a fluid **keeps deforming** under any shear, however small.
examTip.mnemonic: **Solid: stress ∝ strain. Fluid: stress ∝ RATE of strain.** It follows immediately that a fluid **at rest carries no shear** — which is the foundation of all hydrostatics.

questions.stem: A plate 0.5 m² in area moves at 2 m/s over a fixed surface, separated by an oil film 1 mm thick of viscosity 0.1 Pa·s. The force required is:
questions.solution:
**100 N.**

**Assuming a linear velocity profile across the thin film:**

> **du/dy = U/t = 2 / 0.001 = 2000 s⁻¹**
> **τ = μ (du/dy) = 0.1 × 2000 = 200 Pa**
> **F = τ A = 200 × 0.5 = 100 N**

**Two assumptions were made, and both are worth naming:**

| Assumption | Justification |
|---|---|
| **Linear velocity profile** | Valid for a **THIN film** — the profile has no room to curve |
| **NO-SLIP** at both surfaces | The fluid **sticks** to the boundary: velocity **U at the plate, 0 at the fixed surface** |

**The no-slip condition** is fundamental and worth stating:

> A **real (viscous) fluid in contact with a solid boundary has ZERO velocity RELATIVE to that boundary.** The fluid does not slide along the surface; it adheres to it.

**Everything about viscous flow follows from no-slip**: it is what creates the **velocity gradient**, hence the **shear stress**, hence the **drag** on every surface and the **head loss** in every pipe. Without it there would be no boundary layer, no friction factor, and no need for pumps.

**Watch the units**, which is where this calculation is most often lost:

| Quantity | Correct unit | Common error |
|---|---|---|
| Film thickness | **0.001 m** | Leaving it in **mm**, giving 0.1 N |
| μ | **Pa·s** | Confusing with **poise** (÷10) |
| du/dy | **s⁻¹** | — |

**A variant worth knowing — the torque on a rotating shaft in a bearing:**

> **τ = μ (πDN/60) / t** where πDN/60 is the surface speed
> **Torque T = τ × (πDL) × (D/2)**, and **Power = 2πNT/60**

since the shear stress acts over the curved surface area πDL at a radius D/2. The same physics, in cylindrical geometry — and the basis of journal bearing design.

**A second variant — a plate midway between two fixed surfaces**: the shear acts on **both** faces, so the force is **doubled**. And a plate at an unequal distance from two surfaces has different gradients on each face, which must be added:

> **F = μUA(1/t₁ + 1/t₂)**

**The physical reading of the result**: 100 N to drag half a square metre at walking speed over a millimetre of thin oil. Halve the film thickness and the force **doubles** — which is why bearing clearances are specified so tightly, and why a loss of oil film thickness raises friction sharply before seizure.

examTip.trap: Leaving the film thickness in **millimetres** gives 0.1 N — a factor of 1000 out, and it is the commonest slip in this calculation.
examTip.trick: **τ = μU/t = 0.1 × 2/0.001 = 200 Pa; F = τA = 100 N.** Convert every length to metres before you start, not at the end.
examTip.mnemonic: **Force ∝ 1/thickness.** Halve the film and the force doubles — which is why bearing clearances are held so tightly, and why losing oil film raises friction sharply before seizure.

questions.stem: With increasing temperature, the viscosity of a liquid and of a gas respectively:
questions.solution:
**A liquid's viscosity DECREASES; a gas's viscosity INCREASES.**

**They behave oppositely because the viscosity arises from different mechanisms:**

| | **LIQUID** | **GAS** |
|---|---|---|
| Viscosity arises from | **COHESION** — intermolecular attraction between closely packed molecules | **MOLECULAR MOMENTUM EXCHANGE** — molecules crossing between layers and carrying momentum with them |
| Rising temperature | **Weakens cohesion** → viscosity **FALLS** | **Increases molecular speed** → more momentum exchange → viscosity **RISES** |

**The everyday confirmation for liquids**: heating oil, honey or bitumen makes it **runnier**. That is why bitumen is heated before spraying, why engine oil thins when the engine warms, and why lubricant grades specify a viscosity at temperature rather than a single number.

**For gases the effect is counter-intuitive but real**: hot air is **more** viscous than cold air. The molecules are further apart than in a liquid, so cohesion contributes almost nothing; the entire viscosity comes from molecules **wandering between layers** and transferring momentum, and they do that faster when hotter.

**Approximate magnitudes for water:**

| Temperature | μ (× 10⁻³ Pa·s) |
|---|---|
| 0 °C | **1.79** |
| **20 °C** | **1.00** |
| 40 °C | 0.65 |
| 100 °C | 0.28 |

> Water at 0 °C is **six times** as viscous as at 100 °C — a substantial variation, and one that matters when a hydraulic calculation is made at one temperature and the system operates at another.

**Pressure**, by contrast, has **little effect** on the viscosity of either at ordinary pressures — which is why viscosity is normally tabulated against temperature alone.

**Where this matters in civil engineering:**

| Application | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Pipe friction** | Cold water is more viscous → **lower Reynolds number** → higher friction factor in laminar and transitional flow |
| **Bitumen** in road works | Heated to reduce viscosity for spraying and mixing; the viscosity grade is temperature-specified |
| **Concrete admixtures** and grouts | Temperature affects flow and set |
| **Groundwater flow** | **Permeability k = K γ/μ** — so permeability measured in a cold laboratory differs from field behaviour; results are **corrected to 27 °C** by IS 2720 |
| Laboratory permeability tests | Same correction |

**The permeability correction deserves note** because it is a real procedural requirement: the coefficient of permeability depends on the fluid as well as the soil, and since μ varies by nearly a factor of two between 10 °C and 30 °C, the test result must be corrected to a standard temperature before it can be compared or used.

**Sutherland's formula** for gases and an **exponential or Andrade relation** for liquids describe the variation quantitatively, but for examination purposes the **direction** of each effect and the **reason** for it are what is tested.

examTip.trap: "Both decrease" feels right because everyday experience is of liquids. Gases behave the **opposite** way.
examTip.trick: Different mechanisms: a liquid's viscosity is **cohesion** (heat weakens it), a gas's is **molecular momentum exchange** (heat increases it).
examTip.mnemonic: **Hot oil runs; hot air drags.** Practical consequence: permeability depends on μ, so laboratory k values are corrected to **27 °C** before use.

questions.stem: The excess pressure inside a spherical liquid droplet of diameter d is:
questions.solution:
**4σ/d.**

**The three standard cases, which must be kept apart:**

| Case | Excess pressure | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Liquid DROPLET** | **Δp = 4σ/d** | **ONE** surface |
| **SOAP BUBBLE** | **Δp = 8σ/d** | **TWO** surfaces — inner and outer |
| **Cylindrical JET** | **Δp = 2σ/d** | Curved in **ONE** direction only |

**Derivation for the droplet** — equate the pressure force on a diametral plane to the surface tension force around its circumference:

> Pressure force = **Δp × (πd²/4)**
> Surface tension force = **σ × πd**
> Equating: **Δp = 4σ/d** ✓

**The soap bubble doubles it** because a bubble is a thin **film with two surfaces** in contact with air — inner and outer — each contributing σπd. **The jet halves it** because a cylinder is curved in only one plane, so only one radius of curvature contributes.

> The general statement is the **Young–Laplace equation**: **Δp = σ(1/R₁ + 1/R₂)**. For a sphere R₁ = R₂ = d/2 giving 4σ/d; for a cylinder R₂ = ∞ giving 2σ/d.

**Note the inverse relation with diameter:**

> **The SMALLER the droplet, the GREATER the internal pressure.**

That is why a fine mist is harder to produce than a coarse spray (more surface energy per unit volume), why small bubbles dissolve into large ones, and why a droplet's pressure rises as it evaporates.

**Surface tension** itself:

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| **Definition** | Force per unit length at a liquid surface, or energy per unit area |
| **Unit** | **N/m** |
| **Water at 20 °C** | **0.073 N/m** |
| Mercury | 0.51 N/m |
| Effect of **temperature** | **DECREASES** — it vanishes at the critical point |
| Effect of a **detergent** | **DECREASES** sharply — which is how detergents work |

**Its cause**: a molecule in the **interior** is pulled equally in all directions; one at the **surface** has no neighbours above, so it feels a **net inward pull**. The surface therefore behaves as a **stretched membrane**, and the liquid minimises its surface area — which is why a free droplet is **spherical**, the sphere having the least surface area for a given volume.

**Where it matters in civil engineering:**

| Application | Effect |
|---|---|
| **CAPILLARY rise** in soil and in fine tubes | **h = 4σ cos θ/(γ d)** — the mechanism of soil suction and capillary fringe |
| **Apparent cohesion** in moist sand | Surface tension at the menisci binds the grains — why a sandcastle stands |
| **Manometer** readings in fine tubes | A capillary correction is needed |
| Formation of **spray and droplets** | Sprinklers, aerators |
| **Weir flow** at very low heads | Surface tension distorts the nappe, so weir formulae have a minimum head |

**Apparent cohesion is worth emphasis** because it explains a real and sometimes dangerous phenomenon: **moist** sand appears to have cohesion and will stand in a vertical cut, but the cohesion is **entirely due to capillary menisci between grains**. **Saturate it or dry it completely and the cohesion vanishes** — which is why trench collapses in sand so often follow rain or, equally, the drying of a previously damp face.

questions.stem: The capillary rise of water in a clean glass tube of diameter 1 mm is approximately (σ = 0.073 N/m, θ = 0):
questions.solution:
**About 30 mm.**

> **h = 4σ cos θ / (γ d) = 4 × 0.073 × 1 / (9810 × 0.001) = 0.292/9.81 = 0.0298 m ≈ 30 mm**

**Derivation** — equate the vertical component of the surface tension force around the circumference to the weight of the raised column:

> **σ cos θ × πd = γ × (πd²/4) × h**
> **h = 4σ cos θ/(γ d)** ✓

**The key relation:**

> **h ∝ 1/d** — the capillary rise is **inversely proportional to the diameter**.

So a **10× finer** tube gives **10× the rise**. In a 0.1 mm tube the water would rise **300 mm**; in a 0.01 mm tube, **3 m**. This is why capillary effects are negligible in a pipe and dominant in a fine-grained soil.

**The contact angle θ** determines whether the liquid rises or falls:

| Liquid and surface | θ | Behaviour | Meniscus |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Water on clean glass** | **≈ 0°** | **RISES** — wetting | **Concave** up |
| **MERCURY on glass** | **≈ 130°** | **DEPRESSES** — non-wetting | **CONVEX** up |
| Water on a greasy surface | > 90° | Depresses | Convex |

**Mercury is depressed** because cos 130° is **negative** — its cohesion (mercury to mercury) exceeds its adhesion to glass, so it pulls away from the wall. This matters for mercury manometers, where the correction is downward rather than upward, and it is why mercury forms beads on a surface while water spreads.

**The soil mechanics application is the important one:**

| Effect | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **Capillary FRINGE** above the water table | Soil is **saturated but under NEGATIVE pore pressure** |
| **Negative pore pressure → INCREASED effective stress** | **σ′ = σ − u**, and u is negative, so σ′ **exceeds** σ |
| **Apparent cohesion** in moist sand | Menisci bind the grains — the sandcastle effect |
| **Frost heave** | Capillary action draws water up to a growing ice lens |
| Rise of damp in masonry | Capillary rise through fine pores in brick and mortar |

**Approximate capillary rise in soils**, using an effective pore diameter:

| Soil | Capillary rise |
|---|---|
| Coarse sand | 0.1 – 0.15 m |
| Fine sand | 0.3 – 2 m |
| **Silt** | **1 – 10 m** |
| **Clay** | **10 m and more** |

**Silt's high capillary rise combined with reasonable permeability makes it the most FROST-SUSCEPTIBLE soil** — it can draw water up fast enough and far enough to feed a growing ice lens. Clay has a greater potential rise but is too impermeable to supply water quickly; sand is permeable but has too little rise. Silt is the unfortunate combination of both, which is why frost-susceptible subgrade criteria are written in terms of the silt fraction.

**A practical note on the calculation**: the capillary rise in soil is often written **h = C/(e d₁₀)** (Hazen), with C from 10 to 50 mm², recognising that the effective pore size relates to the grain size and the void ratio rather than to any measurable tube diameter.

examTip.trick: **h = 4σcosθ/(γd) = 4(0.073)/(9810 × 0.001) ≈ 0.030 m.** The relation is **h ∝ 1/d**, so a ten-times finer tube gives ten times the rise.
examTip.mnemonic: **Fine pores, big rise.** In soils: sand 0.1–2 m, **silt 1–10 m**, clay 10 m+. Silt's combination of high rise and workable permeability is exactly what makes it the most **frost-susceptible** soil.

questions.stem: The bulk modulus of elasticity of a fluid is defined as:
options: −dp/(dV/V), the ratio of pressure increase to volumetric strain
The product of density and gravity
questions.solution:
**K = −dp/(dV/V)** — the ratio of the pressure increase to the resulting **volumetric strain**.

**The negative sign** is there because an **increase** in pressure produces a **decrease** in volume, so dV is negative; K is thereby made a positive quantity.

> **Compressibility = 1/K** — the reciprocal.

**Typical values:**

| Fluid | K |
|---|---|
| **Water** | **2.1 × 10⁹ Pa = 2.1 GPa** |
| Oil | ~1.5 GPa |
| Mercury | 26 GPa |
| **Air (isothermal)** | **= p**, about **10⁵ Pa** — twenty thousand times less |
| Steel (for comparison) | 160 GPa |

**Water's bulk modulus is high enough that it is treated as INCOMPRESSIBLE for almost all civil engineering:**

> A pressure of **1 MPa (100 m head)** compresses water by only **1 MPa/2100 MPa ≈ 0.05%** — entirely negligible.

**But there are two situations where the compressibility of water is essential**, and both are examinable:

| Situation | Why compressibility matters |
|---|---|
| **WATER HAMMER** | The **pressure wave** travels at the **speed of sound in water**, which depends on K: **c = √(K/ρ)** ≈ **1440 m/s**. Without compressibility the wave speed would be infinite and the pressure rise unbounded |
| **Acoustics / sonar / very deep ocean** | Sound propagation |

**Water hammer** is the practical one:

> **Joukowsky's equation**: **Δp = ρ c ΔV** for a sudden valve closure

For water at 2 m/s stopped instantly: **Δp = 1000 × 1440 × 2 = 2.88 MPa ≈ 288 m of head**. That is an enormous pressure rise from a modest velocity, and it is what bursts pipes and wrecks valves.

**The wave speed in a real pipe is LESS than 1440 m/s**, because the **pipe wall also stretches**, adding to the effective compressibility:

> **c = √(K/ρ) / √(1 + K D/(E t))**

where D is the pipe diameter, t the wall thickness and E the pipe material's modulus. A **flexible pipe (plastic) gives a much lower wave speed and hence a much lower pressure rise** — which is one reason plastic pipes are less vulnerable to water hammer than steel or cast iron.

**Controlling water hammer:**

| Measure | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **SLOW valve closure** | If the closure time **exceeds 2L/c**, the reflected wave returns before closure is complete and the pressure rise is much reduced |
| **Surge tank** | Provides a free surface for the water column to rise into |
| Air vessel / accumulator | A compressible cushion |
| Pressure relief valve | Vents the surge |
| Flywheel on a pump | Slows the deceleration on power failure |

**The 2L/c criterion is the central design rule**: L/c is the time for the wave to travel to the reservoir, and 2L/c the time for it to return. A closure slower than that is a **"slow" closure**, and the pressure rise is reduced roughly in the ratio (2L/c)/T. Closure faster than 2L/c gives the **full Joukowsky rise**, however fast the valve actually moves beyond that.

**For a GAS, K depends on the process**: **K = p** for an isothermal change and **K = γp** for an adiabatic one — which is why the speed of sound in air uses the adiabatic value, **c = √(γRT)** ≈ 340 m/s at 20 °C.

examTip.trick: The minus sign is there because pressure **up** means volume **down**; it makes K positive. **Compressibility is 1/K.**
examTip.mnemonic: **K_water = 2.1 GPa — treat water as incompressible EXCEPT for water hammer.** There the finite K is everything: **c = √(K/ρ) = 1440 m/s**, and Joukowsky gives Δp = ρcΔV. Assume true incompressibility and the wave speed is infinite and the analysis collapses.

questions.stem: In FIRST ANGLE projection, the view obtained by looking at the object from the LEFT is placed:
options: On the left of the front view
On the right of the front view
questions.solution:
**On the RIGHT of the front view** — because in first angle the object lies between the observer and the plane of projection, so each view is pushed through to the far side.

**The two conventions compared:**

| Aspect | FIRST ANGLE | THIRD ANGLE |
|---|---|---|
| **Arrangement** | **Observer — OBJECT — plane** ← | **Observer — PLANE — object** ← |
| **The view is** | **PROJECTED THROUGH the object onto the plane behind it** ← | **Projected onto a transparent plane in front of it** ← |
| **View from the LEFT appears** | **On the RIGHT** ← | **On the LEFT** ← |
| **View from ABOVE (plan) appears** | **BELOW the front view** ← | **ABOVE the front view** ← |
| **Used in** | **Europe, India, Nepal — the ISO convention** ← | **North America** ← |

> **THE MEMORY DEVICE THAT WORKS IS TO THINK OF WHERE THE VIEW 'FALLS' RATHER THAN TO MEMORISE THE TABLE: in first angle, the object is between you and the paper, so looking from the left casts the image through onto the plane beyond — which is the right-hand side.**

> **In third angle the plane is between you and the object, like a glass pane, so the image appears on the near side — the left.**

> **So first angle views are placed on the OPPOSITE side from the direction of viewing, and third angle views on the SAME side.**

> **That single sentence generates the whole table, including the plan's position, and it is far more reliable than remembering four separate placements.**

**THE SYMBOL THAT IDENTIFIES THE CONVENTION IS ESSENTIAL ON ANY DRAWING AND IS WORTH RECOGNISING:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **A truncated CONE is drawn in two views** ← | **Its front view a trapezoid, its side view two concentric circles** ← |
| **In FIRST angle, the smaller circle appears on the LEFT of the trapezoid** ← | ← |
| **In THIRD angle, the smaller circle appears on the RIGHT** ← | ← |
| **The symbol is placed in the title block** ← | ← |

> **THE SYMBOL EXISTS BECAUSE THE CONSEQUENCE OF MISREADING THE CONVENTION IS A MIRRORED COMPONENT, AND THAT IS A SERIOUS ERROR: a part fabricated from a third-angle drawing read as first angle is a mirror image of what was intended.**

> **It may look plausible and be entirely unusable.**

> **With international design and fabrication now routine, a drawing crossing between a European and a North American practice without a clear projection symbol is a real hazard.**

> **So the symbol in the title block is not a formality, and checking it before reading an unfamiliar drawing is a habit worth having — particularly on any drawing whose origin is uncertain.**

> **CIVIL ENGINEERING DRAWINGS DESERVE A CLOSING NOTE BECAUSE THE CONVENTION MATTERS LESS TO THEM THAN TO MECHANICAL ONES: a building plan, a road cross-section or a structural layout is generally unambiguous, because the views are labelled and the geometry is not mirror-symmetric in a confusing way.**

> **Where it matters in civil work is in detailing — a connection, a bracket, a reinforcement arrangement, a precast unit — where a mirrored detail is manufacturable and wrong.**

> **So the discipline applies most to the detail sheets rather than to the general arrangement drawings.**

> **And the practical safeguard, beyond the symbol, is to label every view explicitly — 'view looking north', 'section A-A looking east' — which removes the ambiguity entirely regardless of which convention the drawing uses.**

examTip.trick: **First angle places views on the OPPOSITE side from the viewing direction** — left view goes right, plan goes below.
examTip.trap: **Third angle is the reverse — same side** — so the two are mirror arrangements, and a misread drawing yields a mirrored part.
examTip.mnemonic: **Check the truncated-cone symbol in the title block** — and label every view ('looking north') so the convention cannot be misread.
